report.source_text: Neurological examination revealed joint stiffness, neck pain, arm numbness, arm weakness, and hand weakness. The patient also had restricted shoulder movements and extensive distal and proximal muscle wasting. The right arm was adducted, and the forearm was externally rotated. Muscle strength of the left upper extremity was 5/5; right upper extremity was 2/5, abduction was impaired. Flexion was weak in the wrist, 0/5 on flexion and extension of the fingers. Motor strength of both left lower and right lower extremity was 4+/5. Sensation was decreased in the right upper extremity with complete loss at C8–T1 distribution. Thenar, hypothenar, lumbrical, and interossei muscles were grossly atrophied. The patient also had right-sided miosis. Cerebellar function was normal. His speech was fluent, and cognition was intact.

report.source_text: The patient developed superior vena cava syndrome while waiting for the oncology team’s recommendation. He received radiation; the first two fractions were 250 cGy on a 6-mV linear accelerator using a three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy technique. The dose was reduced to 180 cGy for another five fractions afterward. Radiotherapy was completed in 2 weeks. The total dose delivered to the gross tumor volume in the right upper lobe was therefore 1400 cGy. The patient’s pain improved significantly following radiation. The arm swelling and weakness remained the same.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (right apical/Pancoast tumor)
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 58-year-old African American male presented with a 9-month progressive course of right upper extremity weakness, numbness, and burning pain from the right shoulder to hand, with nighttime pain-related awakenings. Neurological examination revealed severe right upper extremity weakness (2/5), C8-T1 distribution sensory loss with complete loss in the right upper extremity, extensive muscle atrophy (thenar, hypothenar, lumbrical, interossei), and right-sided miosis consistent with Pancoast syndrome. Imaging workup (MRI cervical spine, MRI right shoulder, chest X-ray, and CT chest) identified a right apical mass extending to the supraclavicular region with associated axillary lymphadenopathy and bullous changes in the right upper lung. CT-guided biopsy of the apical mass confirmed non-small cell lung carcinoma, specifically squamous cell carcinoma, with immunohistochemistry showing CK5+, p63+, and p40+ expression and TTF1-, synaptophysin-, and chromogranin- negativity. The patient subsequently developed superior vena cava syndrome while awaiting oncology consultation. He received radiation therapy (total dose 1400 cGy to the gross tumor volume in the right upper lobe) delivered over 2 weeks with significant pain improvement, though arm swelling and weakness persisted.

Right-sided miosis indicating sympathetic nerve involvement characteristic of Pancoast syndrome

Immunohistochemistry profile: CK5+, p63+, p40+ (squamous differentiation markers); TTF1-, synaptophysin-, chromogranin- (excluding adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine subtypes)
